# SK2111 — The null-forgiving operator suppresses nothing

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A `!` stands where no nullable warning could be issued, so it hides nothing and reads as though a decision were made.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| Supersedes | S8970 |

## Why

`!` is the strongest claim a C# author can make — *I know better than the compiler here* — and every reader has to stop and work out what was known. Where nullable warnings are switched off at that position, or where the operand is a non-nullable value type, there was never a warning to suppress: the operator is decoration, it survives every migration untouched, and it makes the file look as though its nullability was thought about when it was not. ⚠ **Not hosted by `IDE0080`, and that was measured, not assumed.** `CSharpRemoveUnnecessaryNullableWarningSuppressionsDiagnosticAnalyzer` ships in the .NET 10.0.400 SDK, and a probe carrying all three shapes reported nothing from it — with `EnforceCodeStyleInBuild=true`, `AnalysisMode=All` and `dotnet_diagnostic.IDE0080.severity = warning`, and with `IDE0090` and `IDE0059` firing from the same analyzer set on the same build to prove the code-style analyzers really ran. `dotnet format analyzers --diagnostics IDE0080` reported nothing on the same files while `--diagnostics IDE0090` reported the control.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
#nullable disable
var length = text!.Length;
```

Write:

```csharp
#nullable disable
var length = text.Length;
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The flow-state half of this concept is deliberately not implemented.** `S8969` — a `!` on an expression the compiler has already proved non-null — was specified, and cut for two reasons that are defects rather than noise. First, a `!` can suppress a *nested* nullability warning rather than a dereference (`List<string?> a = b!;` suppresses `CS8619`), and the operand's own flow state says nothing about that. Second, removing one `!` can make another necessary: in `x!.A(); x!.B();` the second operand is non-null *because of* the first suppression, so a rule reporting both hands `skala fix` a pair of edits that together reintroduce the warning. Neither is answerable from one expression's flow state, so the rule asks a question that has an answer instead. ⚠ **What is left is provable without flow analysis at all.** Either nullable *warnings* are disabled at that position — in which case no diagnostic could have been issued there, whatever the operand — or the operand is a non-nullable value type, on which `!` has never suppressed anything. `int?` is excluded: `!` on a nullable value type suppresses `CS8629`. An unconstrained type parameter is excluded, because it is not known to be a value type. ⚠ **`GetService<T>()!` is declined and reported by `SK2113` instead.** That `!` is not inert — it is the wrong answer to a real warning — and the two rules are disjoint by construction rather than by filter, so no expression can produce both.
